title: Managing Cognitive Load with Mini-Whiteboards
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A secondary teacher writing as SoL in the Wild explains how mini-whiteboards do more than check answers: they let him control how much of a multistep task students must hold in working memory at once. Using a four-part case-study exercise on designing a micro-enterprise, he models one step, supplies the scaffold for that step, has students respond on their boards, checks every response, and then erases the boards before introducing the next step. Keeping reference material such as the pattern table projected makes transient spoken information permanent, so students do not have to remember an explanation while also applying it. He argues that a completed handout is a poor proxy for learning and that permanent records belong in notebooks, while the board is a temporary workspace for practice and feedback. Scaffolding is attached to a specific working-memory demand and then faded, moving students from highly supported execution toward independent coordination of the whole process.
points: Breaking a multistep task into steps on a mini-whiteboard lets the teacher control intrinsic load and remove the extraneous load of seeing every future decision at once.
Students who can see the whole handout often work ahead before understanding the earlier step, producing predictable errors from overloaded working memory.
Projecting reference material such as a pattern table keeps transient explanation available while students apply it to their own examples.
A completed handout shows that students did something, not what they understood, so permanent artifacts should be reserved for work students will need to revisit.
Scaffolds such as sentence frames and concrete examples are matched to a single demand and then faded as students gain expertise.
quotes: Rather than putting an entire complex task in front of students and asking them to navigate it independently, I can break the task into manageable steps, provide and remove the appropriate scaffolding for each step, and keep only the information students need at that moment in their working memory.

Most importantly, students are not simultaneously processing the entire procedure, remembering my explanation, deciding what to do next, monitoring whether they are doing it correctly, and producing an answer.

Students can see everything that they will eventually have to do, even when they are not yet ready to do it. Many students will work ahead, moving into later steps before they have fully understood the knowledge, thinking, or procedure on which those steps depend.

The visual reference does not replace the explanation. Both are necessary but it prevents essential information that students still need in their environment to attend to and select from to enter working memory from disappearing the moment I stop saying or showing it.

A completed handout is certainly visible and collectable, but it is often a poor proxy for learning itself. It tells us that students did something. It does not necessarily tell us what they understood, what they retrieved, what connections they made, what misconceptions they corrected, or whether they could perform the thinking independently.

The important point is that the scaffolding is attached to a particular working memory demand at a particular moment. Students receive support when and where they need it, use it to complete the current step, and then move forward rather than carrying every scaffold with them through the entire task.
The purpose of this entire mini-whiteboard approach is not to keep students dependent on scaffolds or to permanently divide complex tasks into smaller pieces.
